title: Westbrook City Council — Regular Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Six of seven Council members were present (Vice President Shaughnessy absent); every formal vote tonight passed unanimously, but both public-comment periods carried community reaction to a prior meeting's Recreation and Conservation Commission vote. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)

blocks.x: Mayor's Message: Greater Portland Metro's 2027 Budget & Assessment
Presented by Glenn Fenton, Executive Director, Greater Portland Metro

Metro's calendar-year 2027 budget is roughly $23.4 million, a 14% increase over Metro's 2026 budget. (A related but distinct figure, the aggregate increase in municipal assessments across all member communities, was cited separately at 14.4%, though Metro's letter in the packet shows total local funding rising 18.8%, from $6,082,220 to $7,225,588.) Westbrook's own assessment rises a smaller 8.8%, from $908,665 to $988,210. Fenton attributed the increase mainly to wages/benefits (72% of the budget) and fuel/natural gas cost increases (roughly 35% and 65% on new contracts, after unusually favorable prior rates), plus new service he described as fully funded: a Scarborough route and microtransit launched in October (state, turnpike and federal money plus a $145,000 Scarborough contribution next year, at no cost to member communities) and a South Portland expansion due mid-2027 (half federal, the rest through South Portland's own assessment). Excluding those new-service dollars, Metro's expense increase would be about 4.7% ($965,000), though Fenton said that would not have changed Westbrook's assessment. Of Westbrook's $988,210 assessment, $408,540 is TIF-eligible (tied to the Route 3/Husky Line expansion). Of the increase itself, Fenton said about $64,000 is TIF-eligible and about $15,000 would rely on the general fund.

Also reported: a base fare increase from $2.00 to $2.25 (reduced fare $1.00 to $1.10) effective August 1, following a public involvement process; ridership holding roughly flat despite the increase; new credit-card/mobile-wallet payment technology on buses; and an encouraging early trend in the Westbrook High School PASS program aimed at reducing truancy. A Bus Rapid Transit project update is expected back before Council in spring 2027, with a preliminary design targeted for early summer.

Councilor Rairdon questioned the fare increase, calling a 25-cent rise after six years without one modest and citing a 14% increase for the City; Fenton later clarified that Westbrook's own increase is 8.8%, not 14%, which he described as the aggregate average across member communities. Councilor Chau asked whether more member communities joining Metro lowers existing communities' costs; Fenton explained Metro's cost-allocation model is mostly variable (communities pay for the service they receive), so new members mainly help spread Metro's smaller fixed-cost base. Mayor Morse also noted that this year's assessment effectively returns Westbrook to the spending level of the year before last, since last year's contribution fell when South Portland joined. Fenton added that roughly $850,000 in one-time pandemic relief and carry-forward funds in Metro's budget are no longer available. A councilor asked about the TIF-eligibility mechanics (an annual calculation tied to the Route 3/Husky Line expansion) and about the Bus Rapid Transit timeline (addressed above).
Orders of the Day (Second & Final Reading)
2026-118 & 2026-119 — Highway Safety Grant & 41 Brown St. Drainage Easement
Taken together in one motion, without discussion.
Both passed 6–0 by roll call, moved by Councilor Rairdon, seconded by Councilor Chau.
2026-120 — Amending the Land Use Ordinance Regarding Data Centers (Public Hearing)

Finalizes the ordinance that moved through the Planning Board this fall (workshopped Sept. 1, recommended unanimously Oct. 6): data centers are prohibited as a principal use citywide, with small on-site “accessory” server rooms still allowed, and data centers are removed from the list of permitted uses in the Rock Row contract zone (the only zone that previously allowed them). First reading was Oct. 19; tonight's required public hearing drew no speakers.
Mayor Morse spoke in support before the vote, citing concerns about electricity and water demand, noise, and infrastructure burden, and crediting the Planning Board's unanimous recommendation.

“The concerns about standalone data centers are quite substantial — their demands on electricity and water, the potential for constant noise, and the burdens that they can place on infrastructure and surrounding neighborhoods ... Resource-consuming data centers are simply not a good fit for Westbrook. The ordinance being implemented tonight makes a very sensible distinction: it prohibits standalone data centers while allowing server rooms and similar facilities that support an on-site business.”
Liquor License — Sweet Caroline's Retro Lounge, 1 Westbrook Common, Suite 5

A public hearing drew one speaker: owner Caroline introduced her new venue (replacing Westbrook on Tap), describing plans to integrate local art and live music. Councilors spoke favorably, having visited the space.
Approved 6–0 by roll call, moved by Councilor Rairdon, seconded by Councilor Chau.
2026-121 — Retainer Agreement for Fire Apparatus Antitrust Litigation (One Reading)

Authorizes a contingency-fee retainer with Gustafson Gluek PLLC (Minneapolis) to represent Westbrook in the “indirect purchaser” track of a nationwide class action against four major fire-apparatus manufacturers (REV Group, Oshkosh, Pierce, Rosenbauer) and their trade association (FAMA), alleging coordinated price-fixing and production restraint — pumper-truck prices have roughly doubled in a decade and wait times have grown from 18 months to over four years nationally.

City Administrator Angela Holmes explained Westbrook qualifies via its E-One Quint ladder truck, purchased in 2021 through a distributor (delivered 2023 after delay, with price adjustments and a withheld performance guarantee). No upfront cost to the City; fees are contingent on any eventual recovery. Assistant Fire Chief Gary Wagner was present for questions.
Approved 6–0 by roll call, moved by Councilor McCambridge, seconded by Councilor Rairdon.
2026-122 — Authorizing Sale of 12 Water Street (First Reading)

Authorizes selling a roughly 8,985-sq-ft, triangular city-owned parcel to Dori Schulberger of Westbrook for not less than $50,000, proceeds directed to the Riverwalk North project. The parcel came to the City in a 2023 acquisition of former Sappi land along the Presumpscot River; Schulberger's mother had leased the site since 1980 (Scott Paper, later SD Warren/Sappi, at $400/year), placing a mobile home there; Dori inherited the lease and continued paying rent, including to the City after 2023. An independent appraisal valued the largely unbuildable parcel at $50,000. The City retains easements, including for a possible future Riverwalk North extension, though the project's current alignment ends short of this parcel at Garfield Street.

Councilor Rairdon noted this was one of the first constituent issues he heard about after being re-elected in January. Three members of the public spoke in support: Schulberger's attorney Andrew Bratis called it a “win-win”; Garfield Street resident Alice Peterson supported it on the neighborhood's behalf; a third resident praised the public advocacy that helped bring about the resolution.
First reading approved by a show of hands, all in favor, none opposed. Second and final reading scheduled for November 16, 2026.
2026-123 — 2026–2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement, Essential Services Unit (First Reading)

Approves a new 3-year contract for the City's newly created, 12-position Essential Services Unit (Teamsters Local 340), split off from the General Unit in March 2026 to cover employees — facilities, wastewater, grounds, administrative support — whose roles require continued operation during emergencies, distinct from public safety staff. A regional salary study found these positions running 2–11% below market; the new pay scale (effective July 1, 2026) corrects this with an average 5% increase, plus 3% COLAs in 2027 and 2028, a one-time $500 signing bonus per member, and administrative updates consistent with the City's other recent union contracts. Three-year projected cost: $107,837.46, not including scheduled step increases. Already ratified by the union membership; HR Director Joanne Lapolo was present for questions.
First reading approved by a show of hands, all in favor, none opposed. Second and final reading scheduled for November 16, 2026.
Public Reaction to the Recreation & Conservation Commission Vote
Not on tonight's agenda, but raised in both public-comment periods

Three speakers across both public-comment periods returned to a prior meeting's vote to repeal and restructure the Recreation and Conservation Commission into a new committee — a vote on which Councilor Turcotte was the lone dissent. Two thanked Turcotte; a third, who said he supports non-citizens serving, objected to the idea that someone in the country illegally could serve. No councilor responded to either set of remarks on the record tonight, and the matter itself was not back before the Council this evening.

“I think it's no secret that I don't agree with the decision you all made last week, all but one of you, to repeal and replace the Recreation and Conservation Commission ... I'd like to thank Councilor Turcott for her honesty and quite honestly the bravery that she displayed last meeting ... when you put yourself in a position of dissent and then kind of get tried to be silenced, I think it's a clear indicator of how daunting such an act can be.”

“I just wanted to thank Anna [Councilor Turcotte] for the way she spoke up at the meeting ... a lot of people in our community have opinions but will not come out because they're afraid to be judged, and what Anna did last week took a lot of courage.”

“During that public hearing, it sounded as though somebody could be on that committee who was in this country illegally. I think that's a grave mistake ... under the Supremacy Clause you must support and help enforce immigration law, even if you personally or collectively disagree with that ... please make it clear that persons in this country illegally are not allowed to serve in any capacity in our municipal government.”
Larry McWilliams, Planning Board Chair & House District 128 Candidate

Raised two administrative requests unrelated to tonight's votes: that Planning Board meetings not be scheduled on Election Day going forward, citing a recurring conflict for candidates; and that Council/board packets be distributed further ahead of meetings (citing a same-morning delay this week), to give members more time with lengthy agendas. He also asked, referencing the Metro budget materials, for historical data on how closely Metro's past ridership/fare-revenue projections tracked actual results — not answered live tonight.

howMade: This summary was produced from the meeting video (linked above, hosted on the City's Vimeo showcase). The audio was transcribed with AI-assisted speech-to-text and speaker identification. This process cross-checked names against the official city council roster, attributed speakers from context (introductions, roll-call order, direct address by the presiding officer) rather than the raw diarization labels alone, and drafted this summary and the quoted excerpts. Quotes are lightly cleaned of filler words/false starts but not reworded. The meeting continued into executive session (1 M.R.S.A. §405(6)(E)) after the point captured on the source recording; by law, no content from that session is reflected here. Every quoted passage, vote tally, and dollar figure above was checked against the full timestamped transcript, then reviewed and approved by Gerald Doyon before publication.
